name: Feature-against-unit comparison scatter
summary: Two side-by-side scatters comparing one learned feature against another unit — an MLP neuron, or the matching feature from a second transformer — with one dot per token position on the left and one dot per vocabulary token on the right. It is how the paper asks whether a feature is really its own thing, and it reads by the position of a small off-origin cluster rather than by the correlation printed above each panel.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Two suspicions follow every feature the paper describes: that [[dictionary-learning]] handed back a neuron the model already had, renamed, and that the [[feature]] is an accident of one run. Both are comparisons — this unit against that unit — and each is asked twice, because the paper's two model-independent descriptions of a unit are different objects: when it fires, and what it pushes up ([[activation-similarity]] and [[logit-weight-similarity]]).

One similarity number would be enough if two units either matched or did not. They do not. The claim is about the *shape* of the joint distribution: a small cluster far from the origin, where the two units agree about the tokens the feature is supposedly about, and a large blob at the origin where they agree about nothing. Averaging mixes the mode the paper argues from with the mode it declines to trust ([[weight-interference]]). A table of top tokens drops the second mode entirely, so it cannot say whether the agreement is special or typical.

The marginal histograms carry a second argument. The neuron check is about asymmetry, not correlation: whether the *y* axis separates the hypothesised context while the *x* axis does not. That needs both one-dimensional distributions drawn beside the joint one ([[feature-neuron-scatter-plots]]).

### How to read it, step by step

Two panels, the same pair named in both titles. The vertical axis is always the feature under study; the horizontal is the comparison unit — either the [[most-correlated-neuron]], written `A/neurons/489` under the paper's [[feature-notation]], or the matched feature from the second transformer ([[transformer-a-and-b]]).

Left panel: one point per **token position** in sampled data, both coordinates a [[feature-activation]], post-ReLU and so non-negative, running $0$ to roughly $9$–$12.5$. Exact zero is pulled into its own lane before a `>0` break; the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] leaves nearly every token at zero, and undrawn that pile-up would be the plot.

Right panel: one point per **vocabulary token**, both coordinates a [[logit-weight]] on $[-0.6, 0.6]$, each vector slid so its median is zero ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]). The populations differ, so the two printed [[pearson-correlation]]s are not two readings of one similarity and should never be averaged.

Colour is a [[computational-proxy]] score for the hypothesised context — red yes, blue no, sometimes graded rather than binarised. Look first at the small off-origin cluster on the right ([[logit-weight-second-mode]]), then read *down* the y-marginal and *across* the x-marginal on the left. Distance from the diagonal carries the meaning, not spread around it.

### What a bad result would look like

For the neuron check, failure is a tight diagonal in both panels with both marginals reddening together: the feature would be that neuron. For the cross-model check, failure is an unshared red cluster — proxy-relevant tokens strung up one axis and flat on the other.

The round central cloud is not failure on the paper's reading, and that reading does real work: it is what lets a logit-weight correlation of $0.23$ stand as agreement. The label's question mark is the authors' own. Their support is indirect — [[attribution-similarity]] tracks activation similarity — and the extreme case they report, `A/1/3949` against `B/1/3321`, has activation correlation $0.98$ with a *negative* logit-weight correlation, only `.` shared ([[logit-weight-disagreement]]). Without the [[interference]] hypothesis, that same picture says the two features do different things. The converse trap: a high number can come from the untrusted mode, as in fig-32, where the central bulk itself tilts.

### Where it comes back

Three neuron comparisons — fig-16 (Arabic, $0.09$ / $0.21$), fig-32 (base64, $0.18$ / $0.64$), fig-35 (Hebrew, $0.1$ / $0.38$) — read as [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]], consistent with [[polysemanticity]] under [[superposition]]. Four cross-model pairs test [[universality]]: fig-19 (Arabic, $0.91$ / $0.23$), fig-24 (DNA, $0.92$ / $0.46$), fig-29 (base64, $0.85$ / $0.82$), fig-38 (Hebrew, $0.92$ / $0.3$). The gap between the two numbers is wide everywhere except base64. fig-51 reprints fig-19 in Section 5.3.1 to define the two measures a population-level version then applies to every feature.

fig-49 is the shape with the left panel removed: two sibling features from [[feature-splitting]], no correlation printed, and one displaced island — the ten digit tokens, below the diagonal. Watch the labels: fig-16 and fig-32 still say "Feature Activations (Run B)" under a left panel whose unit is a neuron.
